title: Getting a pacemaker fitted | NHS inform
text:
Getting a pacemaker fitted
Before having a pacemaker fitted, you’ll have a pre-operative assessment. The team looking after you will check that you’re fit for surgery. You can also discuss the operation and ask any questions you have.
Some tests may be performed, including
blood tests
and an
electrocardiogram (ECG)
. You’ll also be asked about any:
other medical problems
previous operations you’ve had
problems or reactions you or your family may have had with anaesthetics
You should take steps to improve your overall health such as
quitting smoking
if you smoke and
eating a healthy balanced diet
. This should help speed up your recovery time and reduce the risk of complications.
Read more information on waiting well
Your specialist
A heart specialist, known as a cardiologist will usually carry out the procedure.
If you’re being treated in a large heart hospital, an electrophysiologist may carry out the operation. An electrophysiologist is a cardiologist who specialises in heart rhythm disorders.
Fitting the pacemaker
Transvenous implantation
Transvenous implantation is the most common method of fitting a pacemaker or an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD).
In transvenous implantation, the wires of the pacemaker (pacing leads) are inserted into your heart through a vein. Medication to make you drowsy will be given through a needle into a vein (called a venflon) to relax you and make you feel drowsy.
Tranvenous implantation is carried out under
local anaesthetic
. This means the area is numbed but you remain awake during the procedure.
You’ll feel an initial burning or pricking sensation when the specialist injects the local anaesthetic under your skin where the pacemaker is to be inserted. The area of skin will soon become numb, but you may feel a pulling sensation during the operation.
During the procedure, the specialist will:
make a 5 to 6cm cut below the collarbone and insert the pacing lead into a vein
guide the pacing lead into the correct chamber of your heart using X-rays until it becomes lodged in the tissue of your heart
connect the other end of the lead to the pacemaker and then fit it into a small pocket created under the skin of your upper chest
The procedure usually takes 30 to 60 minutes. It may take longer if you’re having a biventricular pacemaker (with 3 leads) fitted or other heart surgery at the same time. Most people are treated as a day case, which means you will get home that day unless you have complications.
Epicardial implantation
Epicardial implantation is an alternative and less widely used pacemaker fitting method.
In this method, the pacing lead or leads are attached to the outer surface of your heart.
This is called the epicardium. Epicardial implantation is often used in people who have heart surgery at the same time as pacemaker implantation.
The procedure is done under
general anaesthetic
, so you’ll be asleep during it.
The surgeon will attach the tip of the lead to your heart and the other end of the lead to the pacemaker box. This is placed in a pocket created under the skin in your abdomen (below your chest).
This usually takes 1 to 2 hours but could take longer if you’re having other heart surgery at the same time.
Recovery usually takes longer when using this method.
Testing and setting the pacemaker
Once the leads are in place, but before they are connected to the pacemaker, the specialist will test them. This is to make sure that they work properly and increase your heart rate (called pacing). Small amounts of energy are delivered through the leads into the heart, which causes it to contract.
When the leads are being tested, you may feel your heart rate increase or your heart beat faster.
Tell the medical team what symptoms you feel.
Your doctor will decide how much electrical energy is needed to stimulate your heartbeat.
